summary: The note explains how ionospheric disturbances from space weather (solar flares, geomagnetic storms, ionospheric storms, scintillation) disrupt high-frequency (HF) radio used in aviation, maritime, emergency services and broadcasting. It cites incidents in 2023 and 2024 and recommends mitigations: monitoring, frequency adaptation, training, redundant systems, real-time ionospheric data, adaptive technologies, robust signal modes, user education, response plans and maintenance.
one_line: Overview of how space weather disturbs the ionosphere and HF radio, with incident examples and practical mitigation strategies for operators and network managers.
key_facts: The ionosphere is a layer of Earth's atmosphere ionized by solar and cosmic radiation that reflects HF radio waves back to Earth, enabling long-distance communication without satellites or cables.
On October 5, 2023, operators across the globe reported unusual HF communication disruptions, later confirmed by Dr. Emily Hawthorne and Dr. Luis Ortega to be due to a geo-effective solar storm.
On November 12, 2023, a powerful solar flare caused a widespread HF communications outage for several hours, affecting emergency services and aviation networks.
During the March 15, 2024 geomagnetic storm, teams with redundant systems such as satellite phones or internet-based tools were less affected by the HF radio blackout.
After a strong solar event on September 20, 2024, an ionospheric storm caused severe fading and signal disruptions for days.
The NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center is named as a space weather service operators can use to anticipate disruptions.
During solar events, operators are advised to switch to lower frequencies during the day and higher frequencies at night, following the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) principle.
Real-time data from ionosondes and GPS total electron content (TEC) maps gives updates on ionospheric conditions; Brian Chang used such data to adjust communications strategies in real time.
Automated link establishment (ALE) systems automatically select the best transmission frequency and are described as a cost-effective way to maintain HF communications.

Scintillation is rapid variation in amplitude and phase of radio signals caused by small-scale ionospheric irregularities; robust signal modes such as those in digital radio help maintain communication.
Jessica Li led education campaigns that improved operator knowledge of scintillation, especially in high-risk regions near the equator.
Omar Khattab, a network manager, shaped protocols detailing step-by-step measures for various space weather scenarios.
Sarah Stiles, an experienced ham radio enthusiast, emphasizes training and regular drills to enable quick response to changing conditions.
